newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-NEW MARSEILLE PRESIDENT DREYFUS IS NO TAPIE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-NEW MARSEILLE PRESIDENT DREYFUS IS NO TAPIE.

text.p: Like predecessor Bernard Tapie, Robert-Louis Dreyfus, who takes over Marseille's presidency next week, is a businessman.
Like the disgraced entrepreneur -- politician, soccer tycoon and actor -- once did, Dreyfus will chair both France's most talked-about soccer club and sportswear giant Adidas.
But the "soccer crazy" leader, who studied in Harvard, says he has little else in common with the self-made man Tapie, who reportedly decided team line-ups in the place of coaches.
"I'm aware of my limitations. It is out of the question for me to intervene on a technical level or to take part in the shaping-up of a squad," Dreyfus told Reuters in an interview.

His arrival at the head of Marseille turns a painful page for the club, who slumped from being European champions in 1993 to the French second division because of a match-rigging scandal and financial problems.
After the scandal the club was run by the municipality and local councils, who, in the past, have often tried to use the local soccer club as a political stage.
"I did not want to become a table-tennis ball in a political game," said Dreyfus, explaining why it took him so long to make up his mind about taking over the club.
But passion was stronger than reason.
"You can't remain indifferent to Marseille for long," he said.

Despite the risks, Dreyfus decided to go ahead, as he had done in 1992 when he bought 15 per cent of Adidas at the request of the Credit Lyonnais bank, who were worried by Tapie's growing financial problems.
He said he feels at ease chairing both Adidas and Marseille.
"The deal with Adidas was signed before my arrival. Adidas can expect no favour from Marseille. It simply has a five-year contract with the club," he said.
But the new president has high ambitions for the club.
"A lot needs to be done to generate more promotional revenue for the club. Unlike Anglo-Saxon countries, there is not a real soccer culture in France," he said.
Dreyfus believes Marseille should try to cash-in on promotional products such as T-shirts or caps, which make up for 25 to 30 per cent of the revenue of a club like Bayern Munich.
The French club's incoming president should know what he is talking about since he was a member of Bayern's board of directors, a post he will have to resign from to conform with UEFA rules.
"It's a shame. It was fun to sit at a table alongside such personalities as Franz Beckenbauer, Uli Hoeness or Karl-Heinz Rummenigge," he said.
